problem_statement:
*** Problem Statement ***

Consider a $2025\times2025$ grid of unit squares. Matilda wishes to place on the grid some rectangular tiles, possibly of difference sizes, such that each side of every tile lies on a grid line and every unit square is covered by at most one tile.

Determine the minimum number of tiles Matilda needs to place so that each row and each column of the grid has exactly one unit square that is not covered by any tile.
solution:
### Summary ###

**a. Verdict:**  
I have a complete solution. The minimum possible number of tiles is  

\[
\boxed{4048}.
\]

**b. Method Sketch:**  

1. **Permutation of empty squares.**  
   Because each row and each column must contain exactly one uncovered unit square, the uncovered squares form a permutation matrix: there exists a permutation \(\sigma\) of \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\) (\(n=2025\)) such that the uncovered square in row \(i\) is \((i,\sigma(i))\).

2. **Division into left and right regions.**  
   Define  
   \[
   L=\{(i,j):j<\sigma(i)\},\qquad
   R=\{(i,j):j>\sigma(i)\}.
   \]  
   Any axis‑parallel rectangle that contains cells from both \(L\) and \(R\) would also contain the empty square \((i,\sigma(i))\) for some row \(i\); therefore every tile lies entirely in \(L\) or entirely in \(R\).

3. **Lower bound for each region.**  
   *Lemma 1 (left region).*  
   For each row with \(\sigma(i)>1\) the cell \((i,\sigma(i)-1)\) is the rightmost covered cell of that row. A rectangle contained in \(L\) can contain **at most one** such rightmost cell. Consequently at least \(n-1\) rectangles are needed to tile \(L\).

   *Lemma 2 (right region).*  
   Symmetrically, for each row with \(\sigma(i)<n\) the cell \((i,\sigma(i)+1)\) is the leftmost covered cell of that row, and any rectangle in \(R\) can contain at most one of them. Hence at least \(n-1\) rectangles are needed for \(R\).

   Adding the two bounds gives the universal inequality  

   \[
   \#\text{tiles}\ge (n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2. \tag{1}
   \]

4. **Construction attaining the bound.**  
   Choose the identity permutation \(\sigma(i)=i\) (the uncovered squares are the main diagonal).  

   - For each column \(j\) with \(1\le j\le n-1\) place a vertical tile covering the cells of column \(j\) **below** the diagonal:
     \[
     T_j=\{(i,j): i=j+1,\dots ,n\}.
     \]
   - For each column \(j\) with \(2\le j\le n\) place a vertical tile covering the cells of column \(j\) **above** the diagonal:
     \[
     S_j=\{(i,j): i=1,\dots ,j-1\}.
     \]

   The \(2n-2\) rectangles \(\{T_j\}_{j=1}^{n-1}\cup\{S_j\}_{j=2}^{n}\) are pairwise disjoint, each is a legitimate tile, and together they cover every cell except the diagonal squares \((i,i)\).

   Thus \(2n-2\) tiles are sufficient.

5. **Conclusion.**  
   Inequality (1) shows that no tiling can use fewer than \(2n-2\) tiles, while the construction uses exactly \(2n-2\) tiles. Hence the minimum number of tiles is \(2n-2\).  
   For \(n=2025\),

   \[
   2n-2 = 2\cdot2025-2 = 4048 .
   \]

   The answer is \(\boxed{4048}\).

### Detailed Solution ###

Let \(n=2025\).  
Because each row and each column must contain exactly one uncovered unit square, the set of uncovered squares is a permutation matrix.  
Hence there exists a permutation \(\sigma\) of \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\) such that the uncovered square in row \(i\) is \((i,\sigma(i))\).

Define the two regions  

\[
L=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le i,j\le n,\;j<\sigma(i)\},
\qquad
R=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le i,j\le n,\;j>\sigma(i)\}.
\]

\(L\) consists of the cells strictly to the left of the empty square in each row, and \(R\) consists of the cells strictly to the right.

**Claim.** No tile (axis‑parallel rectangle) can contain cells from both \(L\) and \(R\).

*Proof.* Suppose a rectangle \(Q\) contains a cell \((i,j_1)\in L\) and a cell \((k,j_2)\in R\).  
Because \(Q\) is a rectangle, its column interval \([c_{\min},c_{\max}]\) contains both \(j_1\) and \(j_2\); hence it also contains every integer column between them, in particular the column \(\sigma(i)\).  
Since the row interval of \(Q\) contains row \(i\) (it contains \((i,j_1)\)), the cell \((i,\sigma(i))\) lies inside \(Q\), contradicting the requirement that tiles avoid uncovered squares. ∎

Thus every tile lies entirely in \(L\) or entirely in \(R\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Lemma 1 (left region)

For each row \(i\) with \(\sigma(i)>1\) the cell  

\[
r_i=(i,\sigma(i)-1)
\]

is the rightmost cell of that row belonging to \(L\).  
Any rectangle contained in \(L\) contains at most one of the cells \(\{r_i\}\).

*Proof.* Assume a rectangle \(Q\subseteq L\) contains two distinct rightmost cells \(r_{i_1}=(i_1,c_1)\) and \(r_{i_2}=(i_2,c_2)\) with \(c_1<c_2\).  
Since \(Q\) is a rectangle, its rightmost column is at least \(c_2\); therefore \(Q\) also contains the cell \((i_1,c_2)\).  
Because \(\sigma(i_1)=c_1+1\le c_2\), the cell \((i_1,c_2)\) is precisely the uncovered square of row \(i_1\), which cannot belong to \(L\).  
This contradiction shows that \(Q\) cannot contain two distinct rightmost cells. ∎

Exactly one row satisfies \(\sigma(i)=1\); all other \(n-1\) rows have \(\sigma(i)>1\).  
Hence the set \(\{r_i\}\) contains \(n-1\) distinct cells, and by Lemma 1 each rectangle of a tiling of \(L\) can cover at most one of them.  
Consequently any tiling of \(L\) uses at least \(n-1\) rectangles.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Lemma 2 (right region)

For each row \(i\) with \(\sigma(i)<n\) the cell  

\[
\ell_i=(i,\sigma(i)+1)
\]

is the leftmost cell of that row belonging to \(R\).  
A symmetric argument to Lemma 1 shows that any rectangle contained in \(R\) can contain at most one of the cells \(\{\ell_i\}\).  
Since exactly one row has \(\sigma(i)=n\), there are again \(n-1\) such cells, so any tiling of \(R\) requires at least \(n-1\) rectangles.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Lower bound

Every tile belongs either to \(L\) or to \(R\); therefore the total number of tiles in any admissible tiling satisfies  

\[
\#\text{tiles}\;\ge\;(n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2. \tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Construction attaining the bound

Choose the identity permutation \(\sigma(i)=i\) for all \(i\).  
Then the uncovered squares are the diagonal cells \((i,i)\).

*Tiles left of the diagonal.*  
For each column \(j\) with \(1\le j\le n-1\) define  

\[
T_j=\{(i,j)\mid i=j+1,\dots ,n\}.
\]

\(T_j\) is a \((n-j)\times1\) rectangle consisting of the cells of column \(j\) that lie **below** the diagonal.  
The rectangles \(T_1,T_2,\dots ,T_{n-1}\) are pairwise disjoint.

*Tiles right of the diagonal.*  
For each column \(j\) with \(2\le j\le n\) define  

\[
S_j=\{(i,j)\mid i=1,\dots ,j-1\}.
\]

\(S_j\) is a \((j-1)\times1\) rectangle consisting of the cells of column \(j\) that lie **above** the diagonal.  
The rectangles \(S_2,S_3,\dots ,S_n\) are also pairwise disjoint and are disjoint from all \(T_j\) because they occupy complementary rows.

Every cell of the board that is not on the diagonal belongs either to some \(T_j\) (if it is below the diagonal) or to some \(S_j\) (if it is above the diagonal).  
Thus the collection  

\[
\{T_j\}_{j=1}^{n-1}\cup\{S_j\}_{j=2}^{n}
\]

covers all non‑diagonal cells, uses exactly  

\[
(n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2
\]

tiles, and satisfies the condition that each row and column has a single uncovered square (the diagonal square).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Minimality

The tiling just described uses exactly \(2n-2\) tiles, matching the lower bound (1).  
Hence the bound is tight, and the minimum possible number of tiles is \(2n-2\).

For the original board \(n=2025\),

\[
2n-2 = 2\cdot2025-2 = 4048 .
\]

\[
\boxed{4048}
\]
